CO2016B-GE-1.exp: 'To be taken aback' means to be startled or surprised by something unexpected. 'Aback' comes from the nautical sense of sails suddenly pressed back by a wind shift, hence the sense of sudden astonishment rather than anger.

CO2016B-GE-2.exp: 'To give oneself airs' means to behave in a haughty, self-important manner, i.e. to be arrogant. The other options play on the literal word 'airs' rather than the idiom.

CO2016B-GE-3.exp: 'All and sundry' means everybody, one and all, without distinction. 'Sundry' here means various people taken individually, so the phrase covers everyone collectively.

CO2016B-GE-4.exp: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, so the phrase means the beginning and the end, the entirety of something.

CO2016B-GE-5.exp: 'In apple-pie order' means arranged with perfect neatness and precision. 'A sudden shock' belongs to a different idiom and is the distractor here.

CO2016B-GE-6.exp: 'The apple of one's eye' denotes a person or thing cherished above all others, i.e. a much prized treasure. It originally referred to the pupil of the eye, something precious and carefully guarded.

CO2016B-GE-7.exp: 'To put the cart before the horse' means to reverse the proper order of things, i.e. to do things the wrong way round. Option (a) describes 'to build castles in the air'.

CO2016B-GE-8.exp: 'To fall flat' means to produce no effect at all, to fail — as when a joke or a play fails to impress. 'To flatter' is a sound-alike trap on 'flat'.

CO2016B-GE-9.exp: 'To eat humble pie' means to be forced to apologise or admit one's error humbly, which is exactly what follows from empty bragging. The other choices are not established idioms.

CO2016B-GE-10.exp: 'To meet someone half-way' means to compromise, conceding part of one's own position. 'Middle way' is not the idiomatic form in English.

CO2016B-GE-11.exp: 'Of a piece with' means consistent with or of the same character as, so the sentence says this act matches the rest of his conduct. It is also the only option that fits grammatically before 'the rest of his conduct'.

CO2016B-GE-12.exp: 'Not worth his salt' means undeserving of his pay or position, the natural judgement on a man who fails at a critical moment. The phrase recalls the Roman salarium, salt money given to soldiers.

CO2016B-GE-13.exp: 'To make both ends meet' means to manage on one's income so that expenditure does not exceed it — precisely the difficulty caused by a rising cost of living. 'To make matters worse' is a connective phrase and cannot follow 'finds it difficult'.

CO2016B-GE-14.exp: The proverb, from Pope's Essay on Criticism, is 'Fools rush in where angels fear to tread', meaning the rash attempt what the wise and cautious avoid.

CO2016B-GE-15.exp: 'By hook or by crook' means by any means whatever, fair or unfair, which matches a man determined to achieve his object. 'Rest on one's laurels' would mean the opposite of determination.

CO2016B-GE-16.exp: 'To turn a deaf ear to' means to refuse to listen or pay attention, so he ignored the advice. The verb 'turned' also demands this fixed object.

CO2016B-GE-17.exp: The passage opens: 'Everything that men do or think concerns either the satisfaction of the needs they feel or the need to escape from pain', and adds that feeling and longing are the motive forces of all human striving.

CO2016B-GE-18.exp: The passage states that 'In primitive people it is, first of all fear that awakens religious ideas – fear of hunger, of wild animals, of illness and of death'. The author later names this 'the religion of fear'.

CO2016B-GE-19.exp: In the passage the 'being' the human soul forges is one 'more or less like itself' whose favour is sought 'by deeds and sacrifices' through a mediating priestly caste — that is a deity, so the concept of God is presented as a creation of the human mind. Ghosts and witches are nowhere mentioned, so the tempting 'both (a) and (b)' goes beyond the text.

CO2016B-GE-20.exp: The passage says this religion 'is considerably established, though not caused, by the formation of priestly caste which claims to mediate between the people and the being they fear'. Note the careful distinction: the priestly class established but did not cause it.
